Research shows that miscommunication and mistrust is not uncommon between doctors and dermatology patients, and this happens for a number of reasons.​ ​ Sometimes, when we have a bad experience of healthcare, we predict that the same experience will happen again with another doctor. It is not uncommon for people to hold a belief that ‘all doctors are bad’ after a bad experience, or multiple bad experiences.  Sometimes we can feel misheard, and not listened to. This is exacerbated by the lack of time most doctors are able to have with us. Research has shown that if a patient feels dismissed, ignored, or misunderstood in previous encounters, they (understandably) might approach future interactions with skepticism.​ ​ This reminds me of when I was a young girl, I would try to prove that my doctors were ‘wrong’ (that I felt diet and natural remedies worked better than medicine for my skin disorder). This actually stemmed from anger, resentment and disappointment with multiple misdiagnoses, ineffective medication that was repeatedly prescribed to me, and not feeling heard by my doctor when they insisted I was not applying this medication. ​ ​ Research has shown that it is a reality that shame can be exacerbated by doctors through judgement (usually unintentionally), partly as a result of the power imbalance in the doctor-patient relationship (Davidoff, 2002; Dolezal, 2015). ​ ​ You have the right to openly share your concerns with your doctor, to tell them how you feel and to ask them questions or to ask them to clarify their recommendations. I have been apprehensive about disclosing and exposing my own skin condition. Others have encouraged me to show my skin on this account, to help ‘show my followers that I have a better understanding’ of what it is like to live with a chronic skin condition. I partially disagree with this, as I recognise that people respond to their skin in an individual and often unique way. Yes I have an understanding of my own skin condition and how it has affected me, but I would not assume everyone responds in the same way. How you feel about your skin often goes beyond the severity and location of lesions. For this reason I often question social media posts that group ‘common reactions’ within specific skin conditions. However, I do believe that exposing my own skin sets a helpful example to others. When I was younger, I would have found skin diverse social media posts and representation of skin conditions very inspiring and normalising. In addition, skin exposure and the vulnerability it can bring can be empowering. I have not always been open about my condition, and in the past I have kept my skin covered up with my hair or clothing due to shame. I have kept secrets in relationships about my skin, and even missed social events in which my skin would be exposed. I have even made career choices based on how I felt about my skin. Sadly, research shows that this is not uncommon for people who have visible skin conditions. The way we feel about our skin, and how comfortable we feel in our skin can have a large impact on our lives. Keeping an external organ hidden due to shame is difficult and can feel very unnatural. So for the first time, here is a photo that exposes my skin lesions and post inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Hypervigilance refers to an increased state of alertness and awareness that people with visible physical differences may experience due to their condition (the term visible differences can include scars, lesions, burns, birthmarks, disfigurements from accidents, birth defects or illnesses, or conditions like vitiligo or albinism that affect one’s appearance). ​Hypervigilance often occurs when people with visible differences anticipate or are used to receiving negative reactions, stares, comments, or discrimination from others because of their appearance. Sadly, this heightened state of vigilance can result from past negative experiences, or a fear of potential negative encounters.​ ​In hypervigilance, people may constantly monitor their surroundings and the reactions of others, expecting judgement, discrimination, or even hostility. This can lead to increased stress, and anxiety. ​Furthermore, sometimes people start to avoid leaving their home to avoid anticipatory anxiety- this might feel helpful in the short term, but in the long term you can become isolated, and your world becomes very small.​ ​If you feel that you struggle with hypervigilance, @Changing Faces UK have some helpful advice on their website: https://www.changingfaces.org.uk/advice-guidance/coping-with-peoples-reactions/​ If you feel that you would benefit from talking therapy, here is a link to find a local psychology service in the UK: https://www.nhs.uk/service-search/find-a-psychological-therapies-service/ #psychodermatology #dermatology #hypervigilance #skincondition #skindisease #skinconfidence #skintok #skintherapist #skinfluencer #skinacceptance #skinproblems #visibledifference #acne #psoriasis #stretchmarks #burns #scars #alopecia #vitiligo  #eczema #anxiety #socialanxiety #socialanxietyawareness

I won't pretend my Hidradenitis Suppurativa is like a lot of others. Firstly, mine is triggered purely from stress and hormones. Diet change doesn't do a thing. When I was eating the cleanest, I had the worst of flare ups all over my face.  The second thing is my flares up happen mostly on my face. When I was pregnant with my daughter in 2021, doctors didn't take me seriously when I said what it was. They tried treating it like acne, but it wasn't working and my skin grew so much worse. The day after my daughter was born, I had the worst flare up. Midwives in hospital had to get me a dermatologist as I was struggling to talk and eat as the cysts were so big and deep. The dermatologist came down to Transitional Ward and immediately said it was Hidradenitis Suppurativa. I explained I was fighting for my diagnosis of this.  This specific flare up took 4 months after my daughter was born to calm down. I had to stop breastfeeding my daughter, I had to go on very aggressive medication as well as taking other medication thanks to having pre-eclampsia.  I never see Hidradenitis Suppurativa shown on the face. I rarely see doctors mention it happens there. It obviously does, I am proof of it. But it's easy to feel like an anomaly of the disease, as if you're not valid enough or that it's not quite the same. My Hidradenitis Suppurativa happens in other places, more recently in my arm pits and I've always had it in my groin, but it's degenerative, it just gets worse. Psoriasis is an immune-mediated disease (a disease with an unclear cause that is characterized by inflammation caused by dysfunction of the immune system) that causes inflammation in the body. [1] There may be visible signs of inflammation such as raised plaques (plaques may look different for different skin types) and scales on the skin.  This occurs because the overactive immune system speeds up skin cell growth. Normal skin cells completely grow and shed (fall off) in a month. With psoriasis, skin cells do this in only three or four days. Instead of shedding, the skin cells pile up on the surface of the skin. Some people report that psoriasis plaques itch, burn, and sting. Plaques and scales may appear on any part of the body, although they are commonly found on the elbows, knees, and scalp. Inflammation caused by psoriasis can impact other organs and tissues in the body. People with psoriasis may also experience other health conditions. One in three people with psoriasis may also develop psoriatic arthritis. Signs of PsA include swelling, stiffness, and pain in the joints and areas surrounding the joints. PsA often goes undiagnosed, particularly in its milder forms. However, it’s important to treat PsA early on to help avoid permanent joint damage. Symptoms often start between ages 15 and 25 but can start at any age. Men, women, and children of all skin colors can get psoriasis. Scabies is a contagious skin infestation caused by tiny mites called Sarcoptes scabiei. These mites burrow into the skin, leading to intense itching and a pimple-like rash. Here’s an overview of the key aspects of scabies: Symptoms * Intense Itching: Often worsens at night. * Rash: Commonly appears as small red bumps or blisters. * Burrow Tracks: Thin, irregular lines on the skin, usually found in areas like finger webs, wrists, elbows, armpits, and waist. How Scabies Spreads Scabies spreads through direct, prolonged skin-to-skin contact with an infected person, often in close living quarters. It can also spread through shared clothing, bedding, or towels, but this is less common. Treatment 1. Topical Scabicides: Prescription creams or lotions, such as permethrin or benzyl benzoate, are applied to the skin to kill the mites. 2. Oral Medication: Ivermectin may be prescribed, especially in severe or resistant cases. 3. Antihistamines or Anti-Itch Creams: These can help relieve itching but do not kill the mites.
